newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Austria under fire over alleged Iran killings.
newsitem.headline: Austria under fire over alleged Iran killings.

text.p: A week after a German court accused Iran of ordering the 1992 Berlin killing of four exiled dissidents, Austria has come under increasing pressure to reopen a case on the slaying of three Kurdish activists in Vienna in 1989.

A former top Austrian diplomat, Erich Maximilian Schmid, who at the time was head of the foreign ministry's political section, said Austria was bullied by Iran into allowing the suspected Iranian killers to flee after the murders.

Schmid told state television that the Iranian ambassador in Austria appeared at the foreign ministry and "made pretty clear it could become dangerous for Austrians in Iran if Austria brought the suspects to court".
The opposition Green party said at a news conference on Friday that Austria buckled under the pressure from Iran.
The Greens allege that then-Austrian foreign minister Alois Mock was fully aware of the Iranian tactics and gave the go-ahead to allow the suspects to flee.

"We have the documents to prove it," senior Green party member Peter Pilz told reporters. He said his party would publish key documents to force the government to reopen the case and set up a parliamentary inquiry to establish the truth.
Government ministers have repeatedly denied Vienna bowed to pressure from Tehran but the Greens on Thursday published a document they said proved the authorities intervened.
The memo, written by judge Peter Seda, details a telephone conversation with state police chief Anton Schulz wherein he is told not to issue any arrest warrants for the Iranians.
The suspected killers of Kurdish leader Abdorrahman Qasemlu and two other Kurdish activists were never tried. Warrants for their arrest were issued only after they had left Austria.
The Kurds were gunned down at a meeting with Iranian government envoys intended to reconcile the two sides.

Newspapers have said the government held two of the suspects in custody for a short time before letting one board a plane and the other to seek refuge in the Iranian embassy. The third apparently disappeared.

The Greens invited former Iranian president Abolhassan Bani-Sadr to the news conference on Friday to back allegations of government wrongdoing in the Kurd killings affair. Bani-Sadr, who now lives in Paris, said through an interpreter that Austria let itself be blackmailed with the threat that Iran would disclose further details of an arms scandal involving the Austrian arms manufacturer Noricum in the 1980s.

Austria exported arms and ammunition worth 6.8 billion schillings (then around $340 million) to Iran, contravening the country's neutrality laws which ban the export of weapons to countries at war. Iran was at the time at war with Iraq.
Former Austrian chancellor Fred Sinowatz and his foreign and interior ministers were cleared at an arms-to-Iran trial in June 1993 of charges of abusing their office.

But former interior minister Karl Blecha was convicted of tampering with files linked to the case and given a nine-month suspended jail sentence. Several Noricum managers were convicted in 1990 of breaching Austrian neutrality rules and given suspended jail sentences.
